In the previous surah we discussed the impressions that arise in the human heart when it beholds these phenomena. These scenes relate to the great upheaval that the hand of divine power will bring about in this universe. The universe will be shaken so violently that nothing will remain in its place, and this vast cosmos will be turned upside down. There we also explained that the greatest effect of these events is that the human heart turns away from this entire universe and attaches itself to the true Creator, who is everlasting and eternal, and who will remain even when this whole universe is shaken. Amid all these upheavals, earthquakes and destruction, the only refuge for a human being is the court of that Almighty Being, who is steadfast, enduring, and so well ordered that eternity and permanence belong to Him alone. This everlastingness is the exclusive attribute of that Being.

Among the aspects of this great cosmic upheaval is the splitting of the sky. The mention and depiction of the sky splitting and being rent apart appear in several places in the Holy Qur'an. In Surah al-Rahman it says:

﴿So when the sky is split open, it will become red like tanned leather﴾ (37:55), that is, "when the sky splits, it will turn red the way leather turns red." And in Surah al-Haqqah it says:

﴿And the sky will be split open, for on that day it will be frail﴾ (16:69), "and the sky will split open and its fastenings will come loose." And in Surah al-Inshiqaq it says:

﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ (1:84), "when the sky splits." One of the great realities among the hardships and facts of that day of calamity will be that on that day the sky will split apart. Now the question arises: what will be the detailed nature of the splitting of the sky? The truth is that nothing definite can be said about it. We are not aware of its true reality. What we can say is that a great change will occur in the form of this universe that we see, its present order will be shattered, and the present binding that holds all its spheres firmly in their places will be undone.

Here, in this vast atmosphere, the scene of the scattering of the stars also joins the terror of the environment. At present these stars are revolving in their orbits with frightening speed and swiftness, yet they are bound within their own orbits. It is not the case that they run wherever they face in this incomprehensibly vast expanse. If they were to be scattered in the manner that will happen when the Resurrection comes, they would break free from the bond of that very strong, unseen system which holds them together, and they would wander through space the way a speck of dust drifts about in the air.

The meaning of "tafjir" (the bursting forth/exploding) of the seas may be that they will overflow, engulf the dry land as well, and a great flood will come. It may also mean that the water will split apart and take the form of the elements of which it is composed, namely oxygen and hydrogen, just as before the formation of water these existed as the gases hydrogen and oxygen. It may also mean that these two elements too will burst apart like the atom and the hydrogen bomb. One can now vividly imagine what would happen in this universe if atoms and hydrogen were to burst apart, since the atomic and hydrogen bombs that exist today are mere toys in comparison with that explosion, or "tafjir" may have other meanings that are still beyond our understanding. In short, it will be a state of affairs that is great, terrifying and dreadful.

The opening of the graves will also occur as a consequence of these conditions, or the meaning will be that during this vast transformation the graves will actually burst open, and the bodies of people will rise from them so that they set out toward the plain of assembly for reckoning and accounting. The following clause also supports this last meaning.

﴿Each soul will know what it has sent forward and what it has left behind﴾ (5:82). At that time every person will come to know all that they did before and after, meaning what they did earlier and what they did later, or what they did in the world and the good and bad effects they left behind in the world, or what they enjoyed in the world and what they stored up for the Hereafter. The meaning is that after these great events and upheavals, every person will know what they sent forward and what they left behind. Each of these events will be frightening.

Observe the distinctive style of the Qur'an. It says:

﴿علمت نفس﴾ "A soul will know." Here "nafs" means every soul, but omitting "every" makes the statement extremely refined and beautiful. The matter does not end at the point where each person fully acquires knowledge of all their deeds. Rather, this knowledge will have severe effects on the human being. Just as one says, "Fine, you will come to know," although the verse does not explicitly state what the effects on the soul will be, yet these will be harsher than even those great cosmic events. The manner of expression reflects this meaning.

This was an opening that awakened human feeling, consciousness, intellect and understanding in this way. Now, in the next paragraph, there is a comment on the present condition of the human being: how heedless and careless this person is. Here the tone of reproach is extremely compassionate, and within this reproach lies an implicit element of admonition and rebuke. Apparently, the matter is directed toward reflection on God's favours, especially in view of the human being's present creation in a balanced, beautiful and moderate form and shape. It was within God's power to give the human being a form lower than the present moderate and balanced shape and bodily organs, but God gave him a form that is unmatched in both its technical and aesthetic aspects. Is it not incumbent upon the human being to reflect on these things and to give thanks?

Here the human being is addressed in respect of his humanity. It is the quality of being human that distinguishes him and makes him honoured. By virtue of this quality, man has superiority and excellence over all other animals and living creatures, and because of it man has reached a lofty station, and upon him Allah's grace and generosity have been bestowed.

After this comes a warning and rebuke, most compassionate and beautiful. Observe the words:

﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?﴾ (82:6). O human being, reflect: how greatly does your Nurturer and Sustainer honour you? He who bestowed upon you humanity, by which you reflect, grasp matters, and rise above animality. What is it that has deceived you concerning your Lord, so that you fall short and are negligent in the commands of your Lord, and are disrespectful towards Allah, while He is the Most Merciful Nurturer, who has shown you favour and generosity at every step? Among His bounties and blessings, the greatest favour and generosity is this your humanity, and the essence of humanity is that you possess the discernment between good and evil.

After this, the details of this divine honour and dignity are given. First there was a brief call, most effective, hinting and profound in meaning, and there were subtle indications of honour and hidden meanings that were contained in a heavenly call and loving address. Now come the details. In the details are brought the realities of human creation, its proportion, and its extreme balance. Had Allah willed, He could have made man in some other form, but it is purely His grace and generosity that He ordained for man such a beautiful form. If man were to reflect only upon the technical perfections of his shape, physical structure, he would thank Allah; but man not only fails to give thanks, rather he runs headlong upon the path of heedlessness with great arrogance.

﴿O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous, who created you, fashioned you proportionately, and made you balanced?﴾ (82:6–7). This is such an indication that if man's humanity awakens, and his heart and sight are pure, then every particle of his humanity will stir, and his whole being will tremble, because the Creator of man is admonishing him. He rebukes him by recounting His favours, while man lies heedless in the slumber of negligence, living a life full of shortcomings, and indeed is excessively disrespectful towards his Master and Lord, although this Master has given him such a lovely, proportionate and balanced form and personality.

The truth is that to create man in this present beautiful, balanced and proportioned form, and to have all his limbs carry out their functions well, is a reality that requires lengthy reflection and effort, and after such reflection it becomes obligatory to render thanks. It is necessary that man love such a Creator from the depths of his heart and hold Him in reverence, who through this creation has made man honoured. This honour and detailing was purely the grace of Allah, for Allah had the power to create man in any other new form, as He wished; but Allah bestowed upon man this present beautiful, lovely, balanced and proportioned form.

The truth is that in its structure, man is unparalleled. His form is most fitting and balanced, and in the design of his structure there are countless wonders. Allah has given man the power of understanding and perception, and the technical perfections and wonders within his body are beyond his power of comprehension. This creation is more wondrous than the other creations present in this universe.

Beauty, proportion and balance are evident from the human body; the faculties of perception within man are themselves wonders. The human psychology and his spiritual world are even more wondrous, and the psychological and spiritual world also harmonises with his physical balance and proportion.

In the modern age, people have authored many books solely on the physical structure of man, and in them it has been explained in detail what technical wonders lie within human structure. It is not possible to present the complete study here; we shall be content with some indications.

The great systems within the human body, such as the skeletal system, the muscular system, the skin system, the digestive system, the circulatory system, the respiratory system, the reproductive system, the arterial system, the nervous system, the urinary system, the faculty of taste, the faculty of smell, and the powers of hearing and sight: all these systems, if viewed with a discerning eye, are each in their own place wonders. Man has, to this day, invented the most intricate technical instruments, yet they have no standing compared to these systems. When man reflects upon these systems, awe overcomes him and he is struck dumb, yet man turns his gaze away from these great wonders of his own self.

An English scientific journal writes: "The hand is a unique wonder among the marvels of nature. It is not possible for man to invent a device like it. No one can devise a simple instrument like the hand possessing the capacities that the hand has. When reading, man holds the book in his hand, and the hand brings it to the appropriate distance from the eye, adjusting it. This position is automatically determined by the hand. If you wish to turn the page of a book, a finger is placed upon the page with great technical precision, and with slight pressure the page turns. Then we take up a pen, and the nerves of the hand move the pen by themselves. Then this hand uses, in a marvellous manner, all the tools and implements needed for human necessity. Spoons, knives, pens and other instruments come into the grip of the hand automatically, in whatever way we wish. This natural instrument consists of 27 bones and 15 muscles, and it is astounding." (Allah aur Jadeed Ilm, Ustad Abdur Razzaq)

The human ear and its cavity actually consist of about four thousand semicircular arches. These arches are made with great skill and are interconnected with remarkable technical precision. They resemble musical instruments. These arches convey every kind of sound to the intellect and the brain in a wondrous manner. Whether it is the harsh sound of a lightning clap, or the very pleasant rustling of trees, or a harsh voice, or the pleasant sound of musical instruments, the countless ups and downs of the semicircular canals within the ear convey that sound to the brain exactly as it is."

"The eye too is a wondrous instrument; more than thirty million nerve endings that receive light are present within it. Then, for the protection of the eye, there are eyelids and above them a fence of eyelashes. They very gracefully prevent any external object from entering, and they remain in motion automatically, repelling and deflecting foreign things. The shade of the eyelashes also lessens the intensity of sunlight, and the eyelids keep the eye moist by themselves. How beautifully the cleansing system of the eye has been designed! This fluid, called tears, keeps the eye clean at all times, and it is the finest cleansing fluid."

"The system of taste is placed in the human tongue. In the mucous membrane of the tongue there are countless taste cells. These cells are in the form of little knobs. The shapes of these knobs vary: some are fibrous, some are convex, and some are split. These cells obtain nourishment from the muscles of the tongue that swallow and taste. When a person eats something, the taste nerves are affected by this action, and these impressions reach the brain. This entire system has been created at the front part of the human mouth, so that if a person dislikes something he may spit it out. Thus, within the mouth itself, a person determines whether what is being eaten is bitter, sweet, hot, cold, salty or burning. The tongue holds a thousand knobs of taste, linked to the brain through muscles. What is their size, and how do they function? It is an astonishing matter."

"And then the nervous system, which spreads throughout the entire body, is composed of very fine fibres that reach every part of the body. From every corner of the body these fibres join into larger nerves, and they are connected to the central nervous system. If any part of the body is affected in any way, this system informs the central system, even at the slightest change of weather. This system conveys sensations from the whole body to the brain, and the brain issues its command after this impression, and this system performs the task of message transmission with great speed. The speed of this transmission is one hundred metres per second."

"The digestive system is like a chemical laboratory. As soon as anything is eaten, a wondrous process begins in this laboratory, and this factory licks up everything in that bag except the stomach itself. And this process takes place in an extraordinarily astonishing manner."

"We put into this laboratory all kinds of food; we do not see what this laboratory will do with them, nor do we think how this food will be digested. We put meat, fried fish and other foods into it along with some water."

"This laboratory takes the beneficial elements from this mixture of foods: in the stomach these various foods break down in such a way that all their components dissolve. It removes the waste and converts the remaining substances into protein forms, so that they may serve as nourishment for the various cells of the body. This digestive system extracts from this mixture the essential elements such as calcium, sulphur, iodine, iron and countless other constituents, and it takes full care that no useful element is wasted, so that hormones are produced from them, and the material necessary for human life is supplied as needed, and this is done in a most orderly manner. The stomach also stores fat and certain other elements so that these materials may be of use in times of emergency. This laboratory performs all these tasks automatically, and a human being need not think about them nor do any work. Man does not know their causes and effects. We simply put countless things into it, and then we are assured that, in order to sustain our life, the stomach will by itself take up the necessary substances, and will do all the work itself."

When food takes a new form through the digestive system, the stomach carries it to the trillions of cells of the body as their nourishment. There are more cells within a single human body than the entire population of this earth, and every cell demands a different food, which is supplied. Only the nourishment that each cell needs reaches it. These cells then take on the forms of organs, such as bones, nails, ears, eyes, teeth and other organs."

"Thus the stomach is a laboratory more complex than any laboratory created by man, and it has with it a wondrous system of transmission more technical than any human system of transmission and reception; and to this day man has neither seen nor invented so intricate a system, and the system of this laboratory functions with perfect discipline and planning." (All these extracts are taken from the book "Science Invites to Faith.")

Much is also said about the systems functioning within the human body. But in all these systems, animals too share with man in some way, although each of these systems, whether in humans or in animals, is in its own place a miracle. Yet the rational, intellectual and spiritual qualities of man are those in which he is unique, and these are the very qualities concerning which Allah draws man's attention, that they are His great favour upon him.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 82, verses 7–8:

"[He] who created you, proportioned you and made you balanced" (82:7). This address begins with "O man" (Yā ayyuhā al-insān).

For example, the perceptive faculty of man that lies in the intellect ('aql): we do not know its reality. We know only this much, that this perception takes place through the faculty of reason, and the faculty of reason is the instrument of perception. As far as the intellect is concerned, we neither know it fully nor know how this faculty of perception actually works.

How our information and perceptions remain in the brain, we simply assume that this information and these perceptions are transmitted to the mind and intellect through extremely subtle cerebral and nervous fibres. But where does the intellect store it? If we assume that the brain contains some kind of recording tape, then for sixty (60) years there would need to be a tape several million metres long to record human observations over a sixty-year life. We mention sixty years because the average lifespan is generally sixty years. In these sixty years, a person records in his brain countless things: words and meanings, impressions and consciousness, and scenes and observations.

How then do individual words and meanings combine to produce conclusions? How do individual incidents and individual images compose to produce knowledge and culture? This is a separate world, and information transforms into sciences and principles. It takes the form of perceptions and understanding, and through experiences knowledge and science come into existence. These are, in their own place, the wonders of the world.

This is one of the characteristics of man, one that is specific to him, and because of which man is distinguished. But this is not the greatest of man's characteristics. Rather, within man there is also a lamp kindled by the spirit of God, which is called the soul (rūḥ). This soul of man connects him with the beauty of the cosmos, and this very soul links every human being with the spirit of the Creator. It grants man those moments in which he becomes joined to the Supreme Reality, which is in itself unlimited, and in that union he attains some glimpses of the beauty of the Supreme Reality.

Man is also unaware of the reality of this soul. The soul is indeed a great thing; man is ignorant even of the reality of the perceptible things that he perceives. Yet it is the soul alone that grants him those moments and glimpses of joy and felicity, because of which he becomes connected with the higher world even while on this earth. Thus he becomes ready for the eternal life of Paradise, and becomes capable of beholding the beauty of the Supreme Reality.

This soul is a special gift of God to man, and it is because of this soul that man has been called man. And for this reason God addressed him thus:

"O man" — and then rebuked him with such loving reproach.

"What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?" (82:6). This is a direct rebuke from God to man. God Himself calls out to man, and when man raises his gaze, he finds himself standing before God as a sinner, a heedless one, one who does not value God's grace and mercy, indeed as an impudent figure before God. Now God informs him of His great blessing and His grace and mercy, and makes him aware of his ingratitude, his shortcomings and his insolences.

This is a human rebuke: if there is feeling in man, he would melt into water. If man seeks the fountainhead of his humanity, and reflects upon this announcement of God and upon the Being of God, and sees before which King he stands, by how great a Being he is being called, and rebuked, and upon whom this reproach is descending, then the truth is that man would be reduced to melting. Just consider.

"O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous, who created you, proportioned you, made you balanced, and assembled you in whatever form He willed" (82:6–8).

Now the next paragraph explains why man becomes heedless and why shortcomings proceed from him. Their real cause is that he does not believe in the Day of Judgement. It is told that reckoning and accounting are a reality, and that its conditions and scenes will be thus; and that the ends of people will not be equal. This truth is presented with great emphasis.

Yet it is the soul alone that grants him those moments and glimpses of joy and felicity, because of which he becomes connected with the higher world even while on this earth. Thus he becomes ready for the eternal life of Paradise, and becomes capable of beholding the beauty of the Supreme Reality.

This soul is a special gift of God to man, and it is because of this soul that man has been called man. And for this reason God addressed him thus:

"O man" — and then rebuked him with such loving reproach.

"What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?" (82:6). This is a direct rebuke from God to man. God Himself calls out to man, and when man raises his gaze, he finds himself standing before God as a sinner, a heedless one, one who does not value God's grace and mercy, indeed as an impudent figure before God. Now God informs him of His great blessing and His grace and mercy, and makes him aware of his ingratitude, his shortcomings and his insolences.

This is a human rebuke: if there is feeling in man, he would melt into water. If man seeks the fountainhead of his humanity, and reflects upon this announcement of God and upon the Being of God, and sees before which King he stands, by how great a Being he is being called, and rebuked, and upon whom this reproach is descending, then the truth is that man would be reduced to melting. Just consider.

"O man, what has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Most Generous, who created you, proportioned you, made you balanced, and assembled you in whatever form He willed" (82:6–8).

Now the next paragraph explains why man becomes heedless and why shortcomings proceed from him. Their real cause is that he does not believe in the Day of Judgement. It is told that reckoning and accounting are a reality, and that its conditions and scenes will be thus; and that the ends of people will not be equal. This truth is presented with great emphasis.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 82, verse 9:

The word "kalla" is also a word of rebuke and reproach. Through it, one is admonished that the state you are in is not right; your thinking is mistaken. Through it, the speech is shifted from the previous subject to another subject and point. A new matter is brought forward, and this is a style of emphasis and forceful speech. This style is distinct from reprimand, reminder, and portrayal.

"Kalla bal ................ bid-din" (82:9): "No indeed! Rather (the truth is that) you deny the Recompense." You do not believe that you will have to answer for this life, and this is the real cause of your heedlessness, because of which you commit faults. It is never possible that a person who does not believe in accountability for life and in reckoning and reckoning, and yet walks on the straight path, does good, and obeys Allah. Sometimes, the hearts of some people become so pure and clear that they obey the Lord only out of love for the Lord. They do not obey because Allah will punish them or reward them, and they have no greed for any reward at all. Yet such people also believe in the Resurrection, fear Allah, long to meet Allah, and desire to see the Lord whom they love. But when someone denies the Resurrection, he is deprived of the etiquette of life, obedience to the Lord, and light and spirituality. Within his body there is no living heart, and his conscience dies.

You people deny the Day of Recompense, yet in truth you are being drawn toward the Day of Resurrection; the record of your life is being prepared. No deed is lost, and none can escape being recorded. The angels do not forget.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 82, verses 10–12:

﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble recorders, who know whatever you do.﴾ These guardians are spiritual beings from among the angels. They remain with the human being at all times, watch over him, and record the deeds he performs. We do not know how they prepare the record, and Allah has not placed upon us any obligation to know its detailed mode. Allah knows that we do not have the capacity to perceive these unseen matters, and nor is there any benefit for us in knowing the manner in which the recording is made. This knowledge is not among our obligations, nor is it connected with the purpose of human creation. Therefore there is no need to occupy ourselves with it, since it pertains to those unseen matters whose disclosure Allah has not made to us. For us, what suffices is the awareness and assurance that the human being is not left unrestrained, and that Allah has appointed over him agents who record his every word. This is so that he may awaken, tremble with fear, and, while fulfilling the purpose of his life, observe the etiquette of life.

The atmosphere of this surah is one of Allah's favours and His grace and bounty, so the attribute of these angels is mentioned here as ﴿kiram﴾ (noble): they are worthy of honour and possess high station. This is so that the human being may be seized with the fear that noble persons are watching over him. Therefore he should feel shame at the time of committing wrongdoing and vices, because it is part of human nature that when a person sits among dignified and honourable people, he does not commit ugly acts, does not use vulgar words, and keeps his conduct upright. But if a person comes to realise that the noble messengers of Allah are noting his words, he can save himself from countless evils that do not afflict those who sit among the dignified. It is a mark of the Qur'an's excellence that it keeps human consciousness alive and awake, and through the concept of the Day of Judgement and the belief in the recording angels of Allah, it stirs the human being with enthusiasm for lofty thoughts and deeds.

After this, the mention of the end of the righteous and the end of the wicked follows, for the records prepared by the angels and the noble messengers of Allah are very important, and on their basis eternal felicity or eternal wretchedness will be attained.

Surely the righteous (al-abrar) will be in bliss, and surely the wicked (al-fujjar) will be in the Fire. On the Day of Recompense they will enter it, and they will never be absent from it. (82:13–16)

So be certain that this outcome is inevitable. It is a settled end: the righteous will enter Paradise, and the wicked will enter Hell. Barr (بر), the singular of abrar, refers to the person for whom goodness has become a second nature. Good deeds include all those acts that are good, and this quality of goodness is in keeping with human nobility. Its opposite term is of the same kind: fujjar, those insolent and irreverent people who plunge headlong into sinful and disobedient acts without hesitation. Hell is the fitting place for their depravity and wickedness, the appropriate abode. What will their state be?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 82, verse 16:

﴿وَمَا هُم عَنْهَا بِغَائِبِينَ﴾ (82:16) "And they will never be absent from it."

Neither at the beginning of the judgment will they be absent from it, nor will they be able to leave Hell through forgiveness. Thus the condition of the righteous (abrar) and the wicked (fujjar) will be the exact opposite of each other. The conditions of Paradise and Hell will likewise be contrary to one another and face to face. However, the conditions of the people of Hell and the pain of Hell have been described in somewhat more detail.

The original subject was that these people denied the reckoning of the Day of Judgment and used to reject it. Therefore, after describing the events of that Day, the terrors and frightening aspects of that Day are mentioned again, so that it may be understood that on that Day they will be completely helpless. There will be no remedy for anyone, no help or support will come from any direction, and this Day will be so terrifying that you have no knowledge of it. By saying that you are completely unaware of the horror of that Day, this fear is increased, just as it is said that a great calamity is about to come.

In the Qur'an's manner of expression, it is a common style to describe a calamity in an unspecified and unknown way. By this style its terrors are greatly increased; that is, the Day of Judgment's calamity lies beyond human imagination. Whatever dreadful notion of calamity and fear we may conceive, it surpasses even that. Then, by repeating the question, its terror is further increased.

After repeating the question, its features are described in a manner proportionate to its terrors.

This is the commentary of Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation) on surah 82, verse 19:

"The Day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul, and the command, that Day, will be wholly with Allah" (82:19).

That is, human beings will be completely helpless, powerless and incapable. Every person will be concerned only with himself; he will be cut off from everyone, and no friend or companion will be remembered.

"And the command that Day will be wholly with Allah" (82:19). On that Day, the decision will rest solely with Allah alone. The affairs of this world and the Hereafter are in His hands, but on that Day this reality will become manifest. Although in this world some people are heedless of this truth and remain in delusion, on the Day of Resurrection this matter will not stay hidden; it will be visible to all. The heedless, the arrogant and the self-deceived will all see it.

This is the terrifying conclusion of the surah. This conclusion, together with the frightening upheavals of the cosmos at the beginning of the surah, overwhelms human thought and human feeling. These two frightening and shaking situations terrify a person. Between these two dreadful states, the beginning and the end, there is a loving, sympathetic reproach by which a particular person is melted with shame. This is the end of the surah.
